prompt: Which condition correctly finds rows where the column `team` has no value?
explanation: NULL means 'unknown', and nothing equals NULL (not even NULL). Always use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

prompt: What is the order a SQL query is written in?
explanation: You write SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT. (The database actually runs FROM and WHERE first, which is why you can't use a SELECT alias inside WHERE.)

prompt: Table players(id, name, team, position, age).
Return the name of every player on the team 'Comets', sorted by name A to Z.
setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, team TEXT, position TEXT, age INTEGER);
INSERT INTO players VALUES (1,'Ava','Comets','SS',16),(2,'Ben','Comets','P',15),(3,'Cal','Hawks','SS',16),(4,'Dev','Hawks','CF',14),(5,'Eli','Comets','CF',15),(6,'Finn','Jays','P',16);
hint: SELECT name FROM players WHERE team = 'Comets' ORDER BY name;
solution: SELECT name FROM players WHERE team = 'Comets' ORDER BY name;

prompt: Table players(id, name, team, position, age).
Return the name and age of players who are 15 or 16 years old and are NOT pitchers (position 'P').
Sort by age from oldest to youngest, then by name A to Z.
setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, team TEXT, position TEXT, age INTEGER);
INSERT INTO players VALUES (1,'Ava','Comets','SS',16),(2,'Ben','Comets','P',15),(3,'Cal','Hawks','SS',16),(4,'Dev','Hawks','CF',14),(5,'Eli','Comets','CF',15),(6,'Finn','Jays','P',16);
hint: WHERE age IN (15, 16) AND position <> 'P', then ORDER BY age DESC, name.
solution: SELECT name, age FROM players WHERE age IN (15, 16) AND position <> 'P' ORDER BY age DESC, name;

prompt: Which join keeps ALL rows from the left table, even when there is no match on the right?
explanation: LEFT JOIN fills the right-hand columns with NULL when there is no match.

prompt: A player row has team_id = NULL. Does that player appear in the result of an INNER JOIN with teams on player.team_id = teams.id?
options: Only if teams has a NULL id
explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only matched rows. NULL = anything is never true, so the player is dropped. Use LEFT JOIN to keep them.

prompt: Tables teams(id, name, city) and players(id, name, team_id).
Return each player's name with the name of their team, only for players who have a team.
setup: CREATE TABLE teams (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT);
CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, team_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO teams VALUES (1,'Comets','Riverton'),(2,'Hawks','Lakeside'),(3,'Jays','Hillcrest');
INSERT INTO players VALUES (1,'Ava',1),(2,'Ben',1),(3,'Cal',2),(4,'Dev',NULL);
hint: FROM players p JOIN teams t ON p.team_id = t.id
solution: SELECT p.name, t.name FROM players p JOIN teams t ON p.team_id = t.id;

prompt: Tables teams(id, name, city) and players(id, name, team_id).
Return EVERY player's name with their team name. Players with no team should still appear, with NULL as the team name.
setup: CREATE TABLE teams (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT);
CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, team_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO teams VALUES (1,'Comets','Riverton'),(2,'Hawks','Lakeside'),(3,'Jays','Hillcrest');
INSERT INTO players VALUES (1,'Ava',1),(2,'Ben',1),(3,'Cal',2),(4,'Dev',NULL);
hint: Start FROM players and use LEFT JOIN teams.
solution: SELECT p.name, t.name FROM players p LEFT JOIN teams t ON p.team_id = t.id;

prompt: Tables teams(id, name, city) and players(id, name, team_id).
Return the name of every team that has NO players.
setup: CREATE TABLE teams (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT);
CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, team_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO teams VALUES (1,'Comets','Riverton'),(2,'Hawks','Lakeside'),(3,'Jays','Hillcrest');
INSERT INTO players VALUES (1,'Ava',1),(2,'Ben',1),(3,'Cal',2),(4,'Dev',NULL);
hint: LEFT JOIN players onto teams, then keep the rows where the player side is NULL (the anti-join pattern).
solution: SELECT t.name FROM teams t LEFT JOIN players p ON p.team_id = t.id WHERE p.id IS NULL;

prompt: Which clause filters GROUPS after they are aggregated (for example, only players with more than 3 total hits)?
explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters the groups after SUM/COUNT/AVG are computed.

prompt: A column has 10 rows, 4 of them NULL. What is `COUNT(column)`?
explanation: COUNT(column) skips NULLs. COUNT(*) counts every row (10). That difference shows up in interviews a lot.

prompt: Table stats(player, game, hits, at_bats): one row per player per game.
Return each player and their total hits.
setup: CREATE TABLE stats (player TEXT, game INTEGER, hits INTEGER, at_bats INTEGER);
solution: SELECT player, SUM(hits) FROM stats GROUP BY player;

prompt: Table stats(player, game, hits, at_bats): one row per player per game.
Return the players whose TOTAL hits is more than 3, with that total.
setup: CREATE TABLE stats (player TEXT, game INTEGER, hits INTEGER, at_bats INTEGER);
solution: SELECT player, SUM(hits) FROM stats GROUP BY player HAVING SUM(hits) > 3;

prompt: Table stats(player, game, hits, at_bats): one row per player per game.
Return each player and their batting average (total hits / total at_bats) rounded to 3 decimals, best average first.
setup: CREATE TABLE stats (player TEXT, game INTEGER, hits INTEGER, at_bats INTEGER);
hint: Multiply by 1.0 so SQLite doesn't do whole-number division: ROUND(1.0 * SUM(hits) / SUM(at_bats), 3). Add the average to ORDER BY ... DESC.
solution: SELECT player, ROUND(1.0 * SUM(hits) / SUM(at_bats), 3) AS avg FROM stats GROUP BY player ORDER BY avg DESC;

prompt: What does a window function (like SUM(x) OVER (...)) do that GROUP BY does not?
options: It keeps every original row and adds the calculated value next to it
explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group. A window function calculates over a group of rows but leaves every row in the output.

prompt: In `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)`, two rows tie for first. What rank does the next row get?
explanation: RANK leaves a gap after ties (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK has no gaps (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER never ties.

prompt: Table stats(player, game, hits, at_bats): one row per player per game.
Return the player and game number for every game where the player had MORE hits than the average hits per game across the whole table.
setup: CREATE TABLE stats (player TEXT, game INTEGER, hits INTEGER, at_bats INTEGER);
hint: A subquery in WHERE: WHERE hits > (SELECT AVG(hits) FROM stats)
solution: SELECT player, game FROM stats WHERE hits > (SELECT AVG(hits) FROM stats);

prompt: Table stats(player, game, hits, at_bats): one row per player per game.
Return player, game and a running total of that player's hits up to and including that game (ordered by game).
setup: CREATE TABLE stats (player TEXT, game INTEGER, hits INTEGER, at_bats INTEGER);
hint: SUM(hits) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY game)
solution: SELECT player, game, SUM(hits) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY game) AS running_hits FROM stats;

prompt: Table stats(player, game, hits, at_bats): one row per player per game.
Rank the players by total hits (most hits = rank 1). Players with equal totals share a rank (use RANK). Return player, total hits and rank.
setup: CREATE TABLE stats (player TEXT, game INTEGER, hits INTEGER, at_bats INTEGER);
hint: Group first, then rank the totals: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(hits) DESC) works in the same SELECT as GROUP BY.
solution: SELECT player, SUM(hits) AS total, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(hits) DESC) AS rnk FROM stats GROUP BY player;
